concepts.name: Constitutional and Legal Basis of MCC
key_dimensions: MCC has no statutory backing — it is a voluntary agreement enforced through moral authority and Article 324
Distinction between MCC and statutory election laws (RPA 1951, IPC provisions)
Debate on whether MCC should be given legislative force and ECI's position on this
Judicial pronouncements on ECI's power to enforce MCC under Article 324

concepts.name: Origin and Evolution of MCC
key_dimensions: First introduced in Kerala Legislative Assembly elections, 1960 — not by ECI but by state government
ECI's role in expanding and formalizing MCC from 1971 General Elections onward
Landmark expansion during T.N. Seshan's tenure as CEC in the 1990s
Evolution from a 6-point document to a comprehensive multi-section code

concepts.name: Trigger and Duration of MCC
key_dimensions: MCC comes into force the moment the Election Commission announces the election schedule
MCC lapses on the date of announcement of election results — not on polling day
Different durations for General Elections vs. State Assembly Elections vs. By-elections
UPSC trap: MCC does not require Presidential proclamation or Parliamentary approval to come into force

concepts.name: Scope and Applicability of MCC
key_dimensions: Applies to all political parties, candidates, and the ruling party/government (central and state)
Does not directly bind private citizens but binds their conduct through candidates/parties
Applicability in states where elections are not being held when simultaneous elections are announced in other states
Whether MCC applies to Rajya Sabha elections — partial applicability nuances

concepts.name: General Conduct Provisions of MCC
key_dimensions: Prohibition on appeals to caste, communal, or religious sentiments for votes
Ban on using places of worship for election campaigns
Prohibition on using government resources (vehicles, buildings, personnel) for campaigns
Distinction between permissible criticism of policies vs. impermissible personal attacks

concepts.name: Government (Ruling Party) Restrictions under MCC
key_dimensions: Prohibition on announcement of new schemes, policies, or projects likely to influence voters
Ban on using official machinery, government media (Doordarshan/AIR) for partisan coverage
Ministers cannot combine official visits with electioneering
UPSC trap: Routine governance activities are NOT stopped; only new policy announcements are restricted

concepts.name: Model Code and Election Manifesto
key_dimensions: ECI guidelines on election manifestos issued in 2014 — manifestos are now part of MCC
Prohibition on promises that are 'irrational' or that 'vitiate the purity of election process' (Supreme Court in S. Subramaniam Balaji case)
Distinction: Free distribution of goods (freebies) as policy vs. as bribe — ongoing legal debate
Manifestos should be released with costing and source of funding — an advisory, not a mandate

concepts.name: Polling Day and Booth-Level MCC Provisions
key_dimensions: Prohibition on canvassing within 100 metres of a polling station on polling day
Ban on carrying arms, liquor distribution, and cash above threshold near polling booths
Restrictions on exit polls — Exit polls cannot be published until the last phase of voting concludes
UPSC trap: Exit poll ban is statutory (Section 126A of RPA 1951), not just under MCC

concepts.name: MCC and the Media: Paid News and MCMC
key_dimensions: Media Certification and Monitoring Committee (MCMC) set up at district and state levels during elections
Paid news: definition, detection mechanism, and consequences (expenditure added to candidate's account)
Distinction between 'paid news' and legitimate political advertising with proper disclosure
ECI's power to de-certify channels and take action under Cable TV Networks Act vs. MCC

concepts.name: Social Media and MCC: Voluntary Code and IT Rules
key_dimensions: ECI's Voluntary Code of Ethics for Social Media Platforms signed in 2019
Internet companies required to take down MCC-violating content within 3 hours of ECI notification
Silence period: political advertising on social media also covered by the 48-hour silence period before polling
UPSC trap: Social media regulation under MCC is largely voluntary/advisory, not a statutory obligation on platforms

concepts.name: Enforcement Mechanism of MCC: Role of ECI
key_dimensions: ECI enforces MCC through Article 324 — plenary powers of superintendence, direction, and control
Complaints mechanism: Complaint Monitoring System (CMS) and 1950 helpline
Actions available to ECI: censure, warning, disqualification recommendation — but no direct criminal punishment under MCC
Flying Squads (FS), Static Surveillance Teams (SST), and Video Surveillance Teams for on-ground enforcement

concepts.name: MCC vs. Statutory Election Laws: Overlap and Conflict
key_dimensions: Conduct covered by both MCC and RPA 1951: corrupt practices (Section 123), electoral offences (Sections 125–136)
MCC violation ≠ automatic legal disqualification; statutory violation can lead to disqualification
IPC Sections 153A (promoting enmity) and 171 (bribery) overlap with MCC provisions
UPSC trap: Violation of MCC alone cannot invalidate election; statutory violations before or during elections can

concepts.name: MCC and Caretaker Government Convention
key_dimensions: Once elections are announced, the incumbent government is treated as a 'caretaker government'
Caretaker government is expected not to take major policy decisions that could influence electorate
This is a constitutional convention, not a legal provision — no explicit constitutional article
Comparison with Westminster 'Caretaker Convention' — India's version is less formalized

concepts.name: Exceptions and Permitted Activities under MCC
key_dimensions: Welfare schemes already notified and funded before MCC can continue — only new announcements are stopped
Appointments/transfers of officials in essential services are allowed with ECI's prior permission
Diplomatic and national security decisions by government are not restricted by MCC
UPSC trap: Inaugurations of projects already completed before MCC may still be restricted — ECI has taken such positions

concepts.name: Star Campaigners: Definition, Role, and MCC Implications
key_dimensions: Recognized political parties can declare up to 40 star campaigners; unrecognized parties up to 20
Star campaigners' election expenses are NOT added to the candidate's account if they campaign for the party generally
If a star campaigner campaigns specifically for one candidate, expenses are added to that candidate
ECI can withdraw star campaigner status for MCC violations — relevant recent controversies

concepts.name: MCC and Transfer/Posting of Government Officials
key_dimensions: ECI has power to transfer officers perceived to be partisan — exercised under Article 324
District Election Officers, Returning Officers, and police officials can be transferred by ECI directive
State governments cannot make transfers of key election officials without ECI concurrence after MCC
Landmark example: T.N. Seshan era transfers and the evolution of this practice

concepts.name: Criticism and Reform Debates around MCC
key_dimensions: Law Commission recommendation (255th Report, 2015) for statutory backing to MCC
Argument against statutory MCC: would overload courts and slow down election process
2nd ARC recommendation on making MCC legally enforceable
Selective enforcement criticism: perception that ruling party at Centre gets differential treatment

concepts.name: MCC in the Context of Simultaneous Elections (One Nation One Election)
key_dimensions: One Nation One Election would drastically reduce the cumulative duration of MCC in effect nationally
Governance disruption argument: MCC restricts development work — ONOE would minimize this
Coovadia Committee / Ram Nath Kovind Committee (2024) recommendations and MCC implications
UPSC trap: MCC duration is often cited as a governance cost — approximately 3–4 months per General Election cycle

concepts.name: MCC and Electoral Bonds / Campaign Finance Transparency
key_dimensions: MCC requires disclosure of criminal antecedents, assets, and liabilities by candidates (Form 26)
MCC period does not stop legal donation to parties but restricts cash-based inducement
Supreme Court judgment striking down Electoral Bonds Scheme (February 2024) and its MCC linkage
Expenditure limits under RPA 1951 are separate from MCC but MCC reinforces their compliance

concepts.name: MCC and Communal / Identity-Based Campaigning
key_dimensions: MCC prohibits use of religion, caste, community, or language to seek votes
Overlap with Section 123(3) RPA 1951 — corrupt practice of appealing to religion/caste
Supreme Court in Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen (2017): broad interpretation — 'his' religion includes candidate's AND voter's religion
Hindutva judgment controversy (1995) vs. 2017 Abhiram Singh ruling — UPSC frequently tests this evolution
